title: Applied Insights from the Group Project
content:
Stepping into the sixth week of our Information Systems Honours programme, the theoretical frameworks we debated in the classroom were finally put to the test as we commenced our practical fieldwork. Up until this point, our group had pivoted our project focus towards student run hair salons and barbershops operating within our campus environment. We spent hours ideating digital solutions, convinced we had a solid academic grasp of what these informal entrepreneurs needed. However, the requirement to actually conduct face to face interviews and build empathy maps completely shattered the safety of our academic bubble. It is one thing to sit in a lecture theatre and discuss digital social innovation, but it is a humbling experience to look a busy campus barber in the eye and listen to the daily friction of their actual lived reality. When we finally sat down with them amidst the buzzing clippers, I could immediately see a profound sense of curiosity in their eyes. They were wondering what this academic exercise would actually lead to and why we were taking up their valuable time.

This curiosity helped us gain their initial attention, but it did not automatically translate into them giving up the deep operational information we were hoping for. I quickly realised a fundamental truth about informal businesses: when you are operating in survival mode, you rarely feel the pressing need to innovate or drastically improve your current systems. Many of these student entrepreneurs firmly believe that whatever system they are currently using is already good enough. Consequently, during the early parts of the interviews, we received very half hearted answers. They simply could not tell us what they were not complaining about. Even when they did share their frustrations, it was rarely framed as an operational problem that technology could solve. For most of these businesses, their primary objective is just to make money and survive; they do not sit around diagnosing their own workflow inefficiencies. This was a massive reality check. It highlighted the immense difficulty of empathy mapping in the informal sector, where you have to carefully extract latent pain points from participants who do not even view their daily struggles as solvable tech issues.

This fieldwork completely busted one of our groups biggest foundational assumptions. Going into the interviews, we were absolutely convinced that the main problem these participants faced was the immense struggle of juggling their university studies with the demands of their side hustle. As it turned out, we were not entirely far from the truth, but we were definitely not close to it either. We hit the foundation of the problem, but we missed the exact pain point. The reality was that these students actually prioritised their academics quite well and were generally able to manage their time. The actual issue was that their underlying operational systems (specifically how they handled client bookings) were incredibly ineffective. Because their booking methods were disorganised, they could not fully optimise the limited pockets of time they had available between classes. The problem was not a lack of academic balance; it was a lack of operational efficiency that made their hustle far more stressful than it needed to be.

Digging deeper into these constraints, our interviews revealed that the barriers to digital adoption were very different from what we originally hypothesised. We initially thought we would need to design a complex system to handle upfront deposits, assuming that trust and financial collections were a major issue. However, the barbers clarified that this is a once off, cash based business model, and they did not have any major complaints regarding financial communication. The absolute core constraint was simply time. Both the hairdressers and their clients are students bound by strict, clashing academic timetables. The primary friction occurred when time slots got mixed up due to sudden tutorial changes or overlapping schedules. A student is trying to cut hair, but they also need to focus on a pending assignment, while the client is trying to get a fade before a test. This mutual time scarcity made me realise that any digital solution we propose must be laser focused on optimising time slots and managing cancellations, without adding administrative burdens. This perfectly illustrated the concept of strategic fit from Week four.

Listening to these narratives sparked a massive realisation for me regarding traditional technology strategy. In a conventional startup environment, the default technological solution for a small business is to build them a website to market their services. But as I listened to the campus barbers, I realised that traditional tech strategy absolutely does not apply here. They are not looking for a digital brochure to advertise their barbershop. They already have clients within their residence networks; marketing is not their bottleneck. They need something strictly operational, a system that makes their daily execution more efficient. We went into the fieldwork thinking they needed a promotional website where people could book slots, but the act of promotion was entirely secondary to the act of operational survival.

Reflecting on Week six, my perspective on what makes an Information Systems professional effective has matured significantly. The empathy mapping and community interviews forced me to confront the arrogance of designing software from a distance. I learned that a digital strategy formulated without deep engagement is nothing more than an expensive hallucination. Real innovation happens when we adapt our technical knowledge to seamlessly fit into the constrained, messy reality of their daily lives. The insights gathered from the campus barbers reshaped our projects trajectory, moving us away from bloated marketing websites towards a focused, highly operational solution. I am walking away convinced that true strategic success relies entirely on our ability to listen, challenge assumptions, and design with genuine human context at the absolute centre.
